sections.title: SCOPE
sections.summary: Introduces the prologue's purpose: guiding designers on how to measure or estimate shear strength parameters required by the design methods in UFC 3-220-20. Covers the distinction between coarse-grained (cohesionless) and fine-grained (cohesive) soils in terms of pore pressure behavior, and outlines the prologue's organization.
sections.body:
The design methods presented in this manual require shear strength parameters for the soil materials encountered. However, the correct methods to measure or estimate the shear strength parameters are not explained in detail in the forthcoming chapters. The purpose of this prologue is to provide the designer with suggestions on how to arrive at the parameters necessary for successful design and analysis.

The procedures included in this prologue are accepted in mainstream geotechnical engineering practice. There are more advanced theories of soil behavior that are reported in various geotechnical publications, but those are more appropriately applied to designs that are more advanced than those presented in this manual.

This prologue divides soils generally into coarse-grained or granular soils, often called cohesionless materials; and fine-grained or cohesive materials. These distinctions are useful in that coarse-grained soils do not develop significant pore pressures during normal construction loading, while fine-grained soils can show increases in pore pressures for compressive loads and decreases in pore pressures during reductions in loads or excavations.

This prologue is organized by first addressing factors that apply to both fine-grained and coarse-grained soils, and then specifically outlining the methods of arriving at design shear strength parameters.
key_points: The prologue supplements the manual by explaining how to measure or estimate shear strength parameters needed for design.
Only mainstream, accepted geotechnical practice is covered; more advanced soil behavior theories are outside the scope.
Coarse-grained (cohesionless) soils do not develop significant pore pressures under normal construction loading.
Fine-grained (cohesive) soils can exhibit pore pressure increases under compressive loads and decreases during excavation or load reduction.
The prologue first covers factors common to both soil types, then addresses each type's design shear strength parameters separately.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever a designer needs guidance on selecting or estimating shear strength parameters for any soil type addressed in UFC 3-220-20.

sections.title: STRENGTH ENVELOPES
sections.summary: Container section covering the theoretical frameworks used to define soil shear strength envelopes, including Mohr-Coulomb failure criteria and nonlinear envelope representations. Subsections address linear and nonlinear (power function) approaches used in limit equilibrium analysis for geotechnical design.
key_points: Covers both linear (Mohr-Coulomb) and nonlinear (power function) representations of soil shear strength envelopes.
Subsections detail effective stress, total stress, and undrained (φ=0) failure criteria as well as two- and three-parameter power functions.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting or defining strength envelope models for limit equilibrium geotechnical analyses.

sections.title: Mohr-Coulomb Failure Criteria
sections.summary: Describes the Mohr-Coulomb framework used for all limit equilibrium procedures in the manual (pile capacity, bearing capacity, retaining structure stability). Defines effective stress (drained), total stress (undrained), and saturated undrained (φ=0) failure envelopes with associated shear strength parameters and equations. Cautions on inconsistent use of the prime symbol in literature.
sections.body:
The limit equilibrium procedures described in this manual, such as pile capacity, bearing capacity of shallow foundations, and stability of retaining structures, require shear strength parameters that are defined by Mohr-Coulomb failure criteria. In short, the Mohr-Coulomb theory relates the shear strength of the soil to the normal stress on the failure plane. For the case of drained or effective stress strengths, the shear strength is related to the effective normal stress on the failure plane. For the case of undrained or total stress strengths, the shear strength is related to the total normal stress on the failure plane. For saturated soils, there exists a special case whereby the undrained strength is independent of the stress of the failure plane (φ = 0 case). Examples of these three failure envelopes, with the simplifying assumption of a linear envelope, are shown in Figure P-1.

Shown in Table P-1 are the basic shear strength parameters for these three envelopes and the general equation used to calculate shear strength (s) as a function of the normal stress. In geotechnical engineering practice, the prime symbol (ʹ) is used to denote effective stress or drained parameters. In some older references and manuals, a bar above the parameter is used instead of the prime symbol (e.g., φ̄ and c̄). Unfortunately, many papers, manuals, and textbooks are not consistent in clearly indicating drained or effective stress parameters. The prime symbol is often omitted even though the shear strength parameters refer to effective stress or drained parameters, and the reader should be aware of this issue.

The strength equations shown in Table P-1 are simple equations for a line, with the σ and σʹ parameters denoting the total and effective stress normal to the failure plane. For the limit equilibrium analyses presented in this manual, the use of these equations is often embedded into the derivation of the equilibrium equation and is not readily apparent.
key_points: Mohr-Coulomb criteria underpin all limit equilibrium methods in the manual: pile capacity, bearing capacity, and retaining structure stability.
Three failure envelope cases: drained (effective stress), undrained (total stress, S < 100%), and saturated undrained (φ = 0, S = 100%).
Drained strength equation: s = cʹ + σʹ tan φʹ; undrained: s = c + σ tan φ; saturated undrained: su = c.
The prime symbol (ʹ) denotes effective stress parameters; older references may use an overbar instead.
Literature is often inconsistent in applying the prime symbol — designers must verify whether parameters are drained or undrained.
For saturated fine-grained soils the φ = 0 envelope should always be interpreted as a horizontal linear envelope.
figures: Figure P-1 Mohr-Coulomb Failure Envelopes for Effective and Total Stress Conditions
tables: Table P-1 Effective Stress and Total Stress Shear Strength Parameters and Associated Equation for Calculating Shear Strength on the Failure Plane
sections.applicability: Applies to all limit equilibrium design analyses in UFC 3-220-20 that require Mohr-Coulomb shear strength parameters for any soil type or saturation condition.

sections.title: Nonlinear Envelopes
sections.summary: Explains that soil strength envelopes are commonly nonlinear and discusses when a linear approximation (single cʹ and φʹ) is adequate over a specific pressure range. Warns that outside that stress range the linear envelope will overpredict strength, and references Duncan et al. (2014) for four methods to accommodate nonlinearity.
sections.body:
The envelopes in Figure P-1 are linear, and the equations used to calculate the shear strength use the intercept (cʹ or c) and the slope (tan φʹ or tan φ) to calculate the shear strength. Although strength envelopes for soils are commonly nonlinear, a single value of intercept and slope may be accurate enough to represent the strength of a soil over a specific pressure range. Figure P-2 shows a curved envelope, and a linear representation for the pressure range indicated. For the range of normal stresses shown, the resulting shear strength calculated from the values of cʹ and φʹ would be sufficiently accurate for design analyses. However, for normal stresses less than or greater than the range of stresses shown, the linear envelope would overpredict the shear strength. This should be kept in mind when using a design procedure or formula that requires single values of φʹ and cʹ (or φ and c). There are many ways to accommodate nonlinear failure envelopes. Examples of four different methods are outlined in Duncan et al. (2014).

Note: The φ = 0 envelope experimentally determined for saturated clays using the unconsolidated-undrained triaxial test may be slightly nonlinear for a large range of cell pressures, but should always be interpreted as a horizontal linear envelope for saturated fine-grained soils.
key_points: Soil strength envelopes are commonly nonlinear; a linear (c, φ) approximation is valid only over a specific stress range.
Outside the calibrated stress range, a linear envelope will overpredict shear strength — a critical design consideration.
Duncan et al. (2014) outlines four methods to handle nonlinear failure envelopes.
The φ = 0 envelope for saturated clays should always be treated as horizontal and linear, even if slightly nonlinear over a wide pressure range.
figures: Figure P-2 Example Use of a Linear Envelope to Represent a Nonlinear Strength Envelope for a Specific Range of Stress
sections.applicability: Applies when soil strength data indicate a nonlinear failure envelope and the designer must decide whether a linear approximation is adequate for the design stress range.

sections.title: Two-Parameter Power Function
sections.summary: Presents a two-parameter power function (parameters a and b, normalized by atmospheric pressure Pa) as an alternative to linear Mohr-Coulomb parameters for representing nonlinear drained and undrained strength envelopes. Provides equations for both drained (Eq. P-1) and undrained (Eq. P-2) cases, and notes availability in some limit equilibrium slope stability programs.
sections.body:
The use of a two-parameter power function to model the envelope is one method available in some limit equilibrium slope stability programs, which are useful for checking global stability for retaining walls and other structures. Instead of the usual shear strength parameters of φʹ and cʹ, the alternative parameters a and b can be used in the equation below:

s = a·Pa·(σʹ/Pa)^b   (P-1)

where:
a and b = power function strength parameters and
Pa = atmospheric pressure.

Although less common, the two-parameter power function can also be used to represent undrained shear strengths. For example, as shown in Figure P-3(a), undrained strength can be related to the effective consolidation stress as:

su = au·Pa·(σ'con,1/Pa)^bu   (P-2)

where:
su = undrained shear strength,
au and bu = power function strength parameters.
key_points: The two-parameter power function uses dimensionless parameters a and b, normalized by atmospheric pressure Pa, instead of c and φ.
Eq. P-1 applies to drained (effective stress) strength: s = a·Pa·(σʹ/Pa)^b.
Eq. P-2 extends the approach to undrained shear strength related to effective consolidation stress: su = au·Pa·(σ'con/Pa)^bu.
Available in some limit equilibrium slope stability programs for checking global stability of retaining walls and other structures.
The two-parameter form cannot model a shear strength intercept (requires the three-parameter form).

equations.description: Two-parameter power function for drained shear strength: s = a·Pa·(σʹ/Pa)^b, where a and b are power function strength parameters and Pa is atmospheric pressure.
Two-parameter power function for undrained shear strength: su = au·Pa·(σ'con,1/Pa)^bu, where au and bu are power function strength parameters and Pa is atmospheric pressure.

figures: Figure P-3 Other Types of Power Function – (a) Undrained Shear Strength and (b) Three-Parameter
sections.applicability: Applies when modeling nonlinear drained or undrained soil strength envelopes using software that supports power function parameters in limit equilibrium slope stability analyses.

sections.title: Three-Parameter Power Function
sections.summary: Introduces a three-parameter power function (Eq. A-3, after Jiang et al. 2003) for cases where a strength intercept is needed, which the two-parameter form cannot model. The third parameter t is the tensile intercept T normalized by atmospheric pressure. An alternate normalized-cohesion form by McGuire and VandenBerge (2017) is noted as practically equivalent.
sections.body:
Equation A-1 cannot model a shear strength intercept. A three-parameter function is required for cases where an intercept is warranted. Jiang et al. (2003) suggested the following form which is plotted in Figure P-3(b):

s = a·Pa·(σʹ/Pa + t)^b   (A-3)

where:
t = tensile intercept (T) normalized by atmospheric pressure.

An alternate method with a normalized cohesion intercept outside the parentheses was given by McGuire and VandenBerge (2017). For practical purposes, the two forms give equivalent results. A useful summary of nonlinear failure envelopes is found in VandenBerge et al. (2018).
key_points: The two-parameter power function cannot represent a shear strength intercept; the three-parameter form (Eq. A-3) is required when an intercept exists.
Eq. A-3 (Jiang et al. 2003): s = a·Pa·(σʹ/Pa + t)^b, where t is the tensile intercept normalized by atmospheric pressure.
McGuire and VandenBerge (2017) provide an equivalent alternate form with a normalized cohesion intercept outside the parentheses.
VandenBerge et al. (2018) is cited as a comprehensive summary of nonlinear failure envelopes.

equations.description: Three-parameter power function for shear strength with a tensile intercept: s = a·Pa·(σʹ/Pa + t)^b, where t is the tensile intercept T normalized by atmospheric pressure (Jiang et al. 2003).

figures: Figure P-3 Other Types of Power Function – (a) Undrained Shear Strength and (b) Three-Parameter
sections.applicability: Applies when a soil's nonlinear strength envelope requires an intercept term that the two-parameter power function cannot capture.

sections.title: Application of Power Functions in Geotechnical Analysis
sections.summary: Explains practical use of power function parameters (a and b) in geotechnical analysis: software must accept these parameters directly, or they can be converted to equivalent linear Mohr-Coulomb (φʹ, cʹ) values for a specified stress range. Provides a worked example (Figure P-4) and guidance on converting between normalized and unit-based parameter forms (Figure P-5).
sections.body:
To use a power function in analysis, the computer software must be programmed to accept the a and b parameters and correctly calculate the shear strength. Further details for using the power function can be found in VandenBerge et al. (2018).

If the parameters a and b are available, it is possible to estimate φʹ and cʹ for a range of pressures, as shown in Figure P-2 for a curved envelope. Figure P-4 shows an example for calculating the φʹ and cʹ shear strength parameters for the normal effective stress range of 2000 to 4000 psf.

Some analysis methods or software that accommodate power functions may use parameters with units rather than the normalized parameters presented in Eqn. P-1 and P-2. The equivalent parameters can be determined by setting the two equations equal to each other and solving. An example is provided in Figure P-5.

Worked example (Figure P-4): Given a = 0.5 and b = 0.8 (normalized, Pa = 2116 psf):
  s at 2000 psf = 0.5 × 2116 × (2000/2116)^0.8 = 1011 psf
  s at 4000 psf = 0.5 × 2116 × (4000/2116)^0.8 = 1761 psf
  φʹEQ = arctan((1761-1011)/(4000-2000)) = 20.6°
  cʹ = 1011 - 2000 × tan(20.6°) = 261 psf (≈ 0 reported as 261 psf after rounding)
key_points: Software must be specifically programmed to accept power function parameters a and b to use them directly in analysis.
Equivalent linear Mohr-Coulomb parameters (φʹ, cʹ) can be back-calculated from a and b for any specified normal stress range.
Worked example: a=0.5, b=0.8 over σʹ = 2000–4000 psf yields φʹEQ = 20.6° and cʹ = 261 psf.
Some software uses power function parameters with units rather than the normalized forms in Eq. P-1 and P-2; conversion is done by equating the two forms and solving.
VandenBerge et al. (2018) provides further details on power function application.
figures: Figure P-4 Determining Equivalent Mohr-Coulomb Parameters from Power Function Parameters
Figure P-5 Example Conversion between Normalized Parameters and Parameters with Units
sections.applicability: Applies when implementing power function strength parameters in geotechnical analysis software or when converting between power function and equivalent linear Mohr-Coulomb parameters for a defined stress range.

sections.title: Selection of Shear Strength Parameters
sections.summary: Introduces the four general methods for measuring or estimating shear strength parameters (lab tests on disturbed/undisturbed specimens, in situ tests, correlations) and organizes guidance into two deposit categories: in situ undisturbed soils and engineered/un-engineered fill materials. References DM-7.1 for detailed test procedures.
sections.body:
The shear strength parameters for different soil types may be measured or estimated using one or more of the following:
1. Laboratory tests on disturbed, reconstituted, or compacted test specimens
2. Laboratory tests on "undisturbed" or intact test specimens
3. In situ or field tests
4. Correlations

Details regarding these methods can be found in DM-7.1. The selection of shear strength parameters will be discussed for two general types of deposits:
(1) In situ undisturbed soils. These normally would be natural soils, but also can include existing fill soils.
(2) Engineered and un-engineered fill materials. The category would include embankments, dams and levees, retaining wall backfills, dredge materials, etc.
key_points: Four methods exist for obtaining shear strength parameters: lab tests on disturbed specimens, lab tests on undisturbed specimens, in situ/field tests, and correlations.
Guidance applies to two deposit categories: (1) in situ undisturbed soils (natural and existing fills) and (2) engineered and un-engineered fill materials.
Detailed procedures for each method are found in DM-7.1.
Selection of the appropriate method depends on soil type, deposit origin, and design condition.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a method to determine shear strength parameters for any soil deposit type encountered in foundation or earth structure design.

sections.title: In situ Deposit of Coarse-Grained Soil (Sand to Gravel)
sections.summary: Covers the four methods for determining the effective stress friction angle (φ′) for in situ deposits of coarse-grained soil. Lab tests on reconstituted specimens are rarely useful due to inability to replicate field aging/cementation/OCR; in situ tests (SPT, CPT, BPT) are the best approach; correlations such as Duncan et al. (2014) are often appropriate.
sections.body:
The most common shear strength parameter used for coarse-grained soil is the drained or effective stress friction angle (φʹ). Although these materials can have nonlinear failure envelopes, particularly over a wide range of stresses, a single value of the friction angle normally is required at a specific depth for design.

The methods for arriving at an effective stress friction angle for in situ deposits of coarse-grained soils are discussed based on the four methods listed earlier.

Laboratory tests on disturbed, reconstituted, or compacted test specimens – Rarely Appropriate. For in situ deposits of sands and gravel, laboratory tests on reconstituted test specimens are rarely useful. Many important field effects, such as aging, cementation, and OCR, cannot be modeled in laboratory specimens.

Laboratory tests on "undisturbed" or intact test specimens – Rarely Appropriate. Intact samples of coarse-grained soils cannot usually be obtained. Although there are some elaborate methods, such as ground freezing, that can be used, these methods are rare in practice.

In situ or field tests – Very Appropriate. In situ and field tests are the best approach for determining the in situ friction angle of coarse-grained soils. These tests include the Standard Penetration Test (SPT), Cone Penetration Test (CPT), and Becker Hammer Test (BPT). Equations for calculating φʹ from the SPT blow count and qc from the CPT can be found in Chapter 8 of DM 7-1. Both the SPT and CPT can have testing issues for materials much coarser than sands. The BPT has been successful in testing material in very coarse granular soils (Harder and Seed 1986).

Correlations – Often Appropriate. There are many correlations to determine the drained friction angle based on a variety of parameters, such as classification, gradation, particle shape, etc. A large collection of these is found in Chapter 8 of DM-7.1. The correlation developed by Mike Duncan (Duncan et al. 2014) is particularly well-documented and useful. The input parameters are soil type (SP, SW, or GP), normal stress on the failure plane, and relative density. This correlation has an advantage in that the curvature of the strength envelope is considered. A key to applying this correlation to in situ soils is the estimate of the relative density. The relative density can be estimated using the SPT or CPT.
key_points: Effective stress friction angle (φ′) is the primary shear strength parameter for in situ coarse-grained soils.
Lab tests on reconstituted specimens are rarely useful because aging, cementation, and OCR cannot be replicated.
Intact sampling of coarse-grained soils is generally impractical; ground freezing exists but is rarely used.
SPT, CPT, and BPT are the preferred in situ test methods; SPT and CPT can struggle with very coarse materials.
Duncan et al. (2014) correlation accounts for nonlinear failure envelope curvature; relative density is estimated from SPT or CPT.
Equations for φ′ from SPT and CPT are in Chapter 8 of DM-7.1.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the effective stress friction angle for natural or existing in situ deposits of sand to gravel.

sections.title: Engineered Deposit of Coarse-Grained Soil (Sand to Gravel)
sections.summary: Discusses shear strength determination methods for engineered (compacted) coarse-grained fills. Lab tests on compacted specimens are very appropriate if particle size is within ASTM limits. In situ tests are marginally appropriate (QA/QC only). Duncan et al. (2014) correlation is especially useful for coarse soils exceeding lab apparatus limits.
sections.body:
Again, the most common shear strength parameter used for engineered deposits is the drained or effective stress friction angle (φʹ). When it is necessary to provide a total stress friction angle (φ) for an analysis, the effective stress friction angle is commonly used since these are drained materials. The methods for determining the shear strength of engineered coarse-grained soils are summarized in Table P-3.

Laboratory tests on disturbed, reconstituted, or compacted test specimens – Very Appropriate. Laboratory tests are appropriate for engineered coarse grained soils, provided that the test specimen has a maximum particle size within the limits set by the ASTM standards. Examples of triaxial test results conducted on common gravel gradations can be found in Duncan et al. (2007). Some direct shear test apparatuses are large enough to test gravel-sized material. Laboratory test specimens should be compacted to the appropriate dry unit weight expected for the field compaction or placement method. Unless the soil has a significant amount of fines (> 15%), the compaction water content for the laboratory specimens is not critical as long as the specified dry unit weight is achieved. The test specimens should be saturated, and either drained or undrained tests (with pore pressure measurements) can be conducted. Laboratory tests should be conducted at a range of stresses similar to those expected during the operation of the structure.

Laboratory tests on "undisturbed" or intact test specimens – Rarely Appropriate. Not applicable for new fills. Existing fills have the same sampling difficulties as natural coarse-grained soils.

In situ or field tests – Marginally Appropriate. Not applicable for fills, except as used for QA/QC tests on fills. The Dynamic Cone Penetration Test (DCP) can be used for indicating the density of a fill, but no reliable correlations exist for the DCP and the effective stress friction angle. If the fill has been in place for a considerable time, then the methods outlined for in situ deposits can be followed.

Correlations – Often Appropriate. Duncan's correlation (Duncan et al. 2014) is also useful for compacted granular soils. It is especially useful for coarse soils that have maximum particle sizes too large for normal laboratory test apparatuses. The relative density required for this correlation can be determined from the compaction specifications or the compaction control testing.
key_points: Lab tests on compacted specimens are very appropriate when maximum particle size is within ASTM test apparatus limits.
Specimens should be compacted to the target dry unit weight; compaction water content is not critical if fines content is < 15%.
Specimens must be saturated; drained or undrained (with pore pressure measurement) tests are both acceptable.
In situ tests (e.g., DCP) are only marginally useful for engineered fills and are limited to QA/QC; no reliable DCP–φ′ correlation exists.
Duncan et al. (2014) correlation is especially valuable when particle size exceeds laboratory apparatus limits.
Relative density for the Duncan correlation can be derived from compaction specifications or control testing.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the drained friction angle for newly placed or existing compacted coarse-grained fill materials.

sections.title: In situ Deposit of Fine-Grained Soil
sections.summary: Container section introducing the framework for selecting shear strength parameters for in situ fine-grained soils. Distinguishes between undrained and drained strength applicability based on saturation state, loading duration, and pore pressure conditions. Refers to subsections for clayey soils and low-plasticity silts.
sections.body:
For in situ deposits of saturated fine-grained soils, the methods used depend on whether drained or undrained strengths are appropriate. Undrained strengths are generally important when the stability for short term conditions is required, particular if the project loading increases the pore water pressure.

For partially saturated fine-grained soils, undrained strengths are often necessary for locations above the phreatic surface. The appropriate undrained strength characterization is a c-φ envelope. Often in engineering practice, the soil is characterized with an su for an assumed φ = 0 condition. This is not ideal, but as long as the value of su is interpreted using a conservative method, it should suffice.

Drained strength parameters are appropriate for long-term conditions where the pore water pressures can be measured, calculated, or estimated with reasonable accuracy. An example of this would be when increases or decreases in pore water pressure caused by the project loading have dissipated, and the pore water pressures have returned to hydrostatic conditions. A second example would be when a steady-state seepage condition has been achieved, and pore water pressures can be calculated. Drained strength parameters are often assigned to partially-saturated soils above the phreatic surface.

The next two sections discuss methods to determine undrained shear strengths and drained shear strength of fine-grained soils, particularly those which behave in a clay-like manner and classify as lean clay, fat clay, or elastic silt. Nonplastic and low plasticity silts behave differently and are discussed in the third section.
key_points: For saturated fine-grained soils, choice between undrained and drained strength depends on loading rate and pore pressure dissipation.
Undrained strength (φ=0, su) is appropriate for short-term stability or when loading increases pore pressure.
For partially saturated soils above the phreatic surface, a c-φ undrained envelope is most appropriate; using su with φ=0 is conservative.
Drained parameters apply when pore pressures have returned to hydrostatic or steady-state seepage conditions.
Clay-like soils (lean clay, fat clay, elastic silt) are addressed in P-3.3.1 and P-3.3.2; nonplastic/low plasticity silts in P-3.3.3.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting between undrained and drained shear strength approaches for in situ natural fine-grained soil deposits.

sections.title: Undrained Shear Strength - In situ Deposit of Fine-Grained Soil
sections.summary: Describes methods for determining the undrained shear strength (su) distribution with depth for saturated in situ fine-grained soils using a φ=0 model. Covers lab tests on disturbed/undisturbed specimens (LMVT, fall cone, UU triaxial, DSS/SHANSEP) and field tests (VST, CPT). Correlations have limited utility except for SHANSEP and CPT-based methods.
sections.body:
The design procedures in this manual may require the distribution of undrained strength versus depth for saturated, fine-grained deposits. This strength is associated with a φ = 0 strength model. Figure P-6 shows an example stratigraphy and shear strength distribution. The goal is often to have enough data points to represent the strength distribution with accuracy. The methods to determine the value of undrained strength versus depth are summarized in Table P-4.

Laboratory tests on disturbed, reconstituted, or compacted test specimens – Marginally Appropriate. The only value of testing disturbed specimens is to determine the undrained strength for normally consolidated conditions. These tests, conducted on carefully remolded samples, could provide a lower bound undrained strength. However, the resulting strengths do not allow the undrained strength versus depth relationship to be accurately determined for in situ conditions.

Laboratory tests on "undisturbed" or intact test specimens – Very Appropriate. Applicable tests include: (1) Laboratory miniature vane shear test (LMVT) – best for su < 1400 psf, especially soft soils (su < 500 psf). (2) Fall cone tests (FC) – works best on soft clays; no ASTM standard but Norwegian and German standards exist. (3) UU triaxial test – most common; confining pressures should bracket the minor total stress at the sample location; saturated specimens should yield a horizontal envelope. CU triaxial tests produce su values that are too high. (4) Direct Simple Shear Test (DSS) – The Bjerrum Method consolidates specimens to the vertical effective stress; the SHANSEP method (Ladd and DeGroot 2003) uses the preconsolidation pressure profile and an undrained strength ratio vs. OCR relationship.

In situ or field tests – Very Appropriate. For deposits with su < 2000 psf, the Vane Shear Test (VST) is probably the best overall test method; data should be corrected for strain-rate effects per ASTM. The CPT is often used; methods relying on tip resistance (qc or qt) are most reliable. The SPT is considered unreliable for this purpose.

Correlations – Sometimes Appropriate. Several correlations exist for remolded clays or normally consolidated state undrained strength, but have limited practical value. Correlations relying on the preconsolidation pressure profile are available. SHANSEP and CPT Nc/Nk/Nkt methods are site-specific correlations.
key_points: Undrained strength distribution with depth (φ=0 model) is required for many design procedures for saturated fine-grained deposits.
UU triaxial tests on intact specimens are the most common lab method; CU triaxial tests overestimate su and should not be used for this purpose.
LMVT is well-suited for su < 1400 psf; especially valuable for soft soils (su < 500 psf).
DSS with the SHANSEP method links su to the preconsolidation pressure profile and OCR.
Field VST is best overall for su < 2000 psf; CPT tip resistance (qc or qt) methods are most reliable among CPT approaches.
SPT is considered unreliable for undrained strength of fine-grained soils.
Correlations are only sometimes appropriate; most useful when linked to preconsolidation pressure or interpreted via SHANSEP/CPT factor methods.
figures: Figure P-6
sections.applicability: Applies when establishing an undrained shear strength (su) vs. depth profile for saturated in situ fine-grained deposits using a φ=0 analysis.

sections.title: Drained Strength - In situ Deposit of Fine-Grained Soil
sections.summary: Explains the three drained strength envelopes for fine-grained soils—peak (c′p, φ′p), fully softened (φ′FS), and residual (φ′r)—and specifies which envelope applies based on soil plasticity, fissuring, and stress history. Lab tests on intact or remolded specimens are appropriate; field tests are not useful for drained strength.
sections.body:
Three sets of drained strength parameters can be measured for fine-grained soils. These are shown for direct shear test results in Figure P-7. If the soil is initially overconsolidated in situ, then an envelope results from plotting the peak strengths. This is shown as the upper envelope in Figure P-7, with the indicated shear strength parameters cʹp and φʹp. A second strength envelope can be determined if the test specimens are remolded, loaded to normally consolidated conditions, and then sheared. This results in the fully softened envelope shown with a friction angle defined as φʹFS in Figure P-7. The effective stress cohesion for the fully softened condition is normally equal to zero, or the fully softened envelope is nonlinear and passes through the origin. The third envelope is obtained by shearing undisturbed or remolded test specimens to very high displacements, and this produces the residual strength envelope, with a drained friction angle of φʹr. The residual strength envelope is expected to pass through the origin.

The peak strength envelope is often used for fine-grained soils having PI < 20 and LL < 40 that are relatively free of fissures. The peak shear strength parameters depend on the preconsolidation pressure of the test specimens.

The fully softened strength envelope is used for soils that do contain fissures and have a PI > 20 and LL > 40 (Castellanos et al. 2016). This envelope is particularly appropriate for stability assessment of in situ fine-grained soils where the stresses have been reduced due to excavation. The fully softened envelope is also used for clays that are essentially normally consolidated in situ.

The residual strength envelope is used when there has been large displacement due to a shear failure, and the residual condition has been achieved.

Laboratory tests on disturbed, reconstituted, or compacted test specimens – Often Appropriate. Test specimens prepared in the laboratory are useful for determining fully softened and residual shear strengths. The best test methods for fully softened strengths are the direct shear test and the CU triaxial compression test. The best test method for residual shear strength is the ring shear test. Specimens are prepared to a water content at or above the liquid limit and consolidated to the desired test stresses prior to shearing.

Laboratory tests on "undisturbed" or intact test specimens – Often Appropriate. Intact specimens are required to measure peak drained shear strength. The best test methods are the direct shear test and CU triaxial compression test. Test specimens should be consolidated to a range of test stresses bracketing the effective normal stresses anticipated in the analysis.

In situ or field tests – Rarely Appropriate. Field tests are not useful for drained strength of fine-grained soils. Accurate measurement of drained strength requires knowledge of pore pressure during shearing, which cannot be determined accurately by in situ test methods.

Correlations – Sometimes Appropriate. Correlations are not useful for peak drained shear strength due to dependence on preconsolidation stress. Chapter 8 of DM-7.1 presents correlations between index properties (LL, PI, clay fraction) and fully softened and residual shear strength. These are useful for preliminary analysis, checking lab results, and limited design with limited failure consequences.
key_points: Three drained envelopes exist: peak (c′p, φ′p), fully softened (φ′FS, c′=0), and residual (φ′r, through origin).
Peak envelope applies to soils with PI < 20 and LL < 40 that are relatively free of fissures.
Fully softened envelope applies to fissured soils with PI > 20 and LL > 40, excavation-unloaded soils, and normally consolidated clays.
Residual envelope applies only after large-displacement shear failure has occurred.
Direct shear and CU triaxial tests are best for peak and fully softened strengths; ring shear is best for residual strength.
Field tests are rarely appropriate for drained strength because pore pressures during shearing cannot be accurately determined in situ.
Index property correlations (LL, PI, clay fraction) are useful for fully softened and residual strengths in preliminary analyses.

sections.applicability: Applies when selecting peak, fully softened, or residual drained strength parameters for in situ fine-grained soil based on plasticity, fissuring, and displacement history.

sections.title: In situ Deposit of Nonplastic or Low Plasticity Silt
sections.summary: Addresses the unique characterization challenges of low plasticity silts (PI < 10, LL < 50). These soils are dilatant, easily disturbed, and difficult to sample and test. Drainage behavior depends on cv; φ′ typically ranges 35–40°. Provides USR formulas for various failure modes assuming zero excess pore pressure at failure.
sections.body:
Silt deposits with low plasticity (i.e., PI < 10 and LL < 50) require different types of characterization than clayey fine-grained soils. These silts are very dilatant and easily disturbed, which makes them extremely hard to sample and test in the laboratory. Compared to clays with similar liquid limit, the silts tend to be stronger and much less compressible (Brandon et al. 2006). Consolidation tests on low plasticity silts are difficult to interpret and show little effect of preconsolidation, likely due to sampling disturbance.

If it can be determined, the coefficient of consolidation can be used to determine how the silt will behave when loaded. Silts with lower cv (1 to 10 ft2/day) will retain excess pore pressures for significant time periods and behave in an undrained manner. Silts with higher values of cv (greater than 100 ft2/day) will dissipate excess pore pressures quickly and will behave mostly in a drained manner. Low plasticity silts typically have effective stress friction angles in the range of 35 to 40 degrees with little to no cohesion intercept (Duncan et al. 2014). This indicates that low plasticity silts are relatively competent soils, provided confining stress is maintained.

Laboratory tests on disturbed, reconstituted, or compacted test specimens – Often Appropriate. Undrained: CU triaxial compression tests; dilative tendency creates large negative excess pore pressures requiring elevated back pressures to prevent cavitation. Recommended failure criterion: point where excess pore pressure is zero (Āf = 0). Drained: CU triaxial compression tests; effects of disturbance are less pronounced on drained strength.

Laboratory tests on "undisturbed" or intact test specimens – Marginally Appropriate. High-quality undisturbed specimens are extremely difficult to obtain. UU triaxial tests are not advised due to substantial scatter from disturbance.

In situ or field tests – Rarely Appropriate. Intermediate cv values make it difficult to determine drainage condition during testing, making results difficult to interpret. Correlations developed for sand and clay have been shown to be unreliable for low plasticity silt.

Correlations – Marginally Appropriate. Published correlations are not available for low plasticity silts. Typical values of undrained strength ratio (USR = su / σʹvc) can sometimes be used. Assuming zero excess pore pressure at failure and cʹ = 0:
• ICU triaxial compression: USR = sin φʹ / (1 – sin φʹ)
• ACU triaxial compression: USR = sin φʹ
• DSS: USR = sin φʹ – 0.5 sin2 φʹ
key_points: Low plasticity silts (PI < 10, LL < 50) are dilatant and highly disturbance-sensitive; high-quality undisturbed sampling is extremely difficult.
Drainage behavior during loading depends on cv: cv = 1–10 ft²/day → undrained behavior; cv > 100 ft²/day → drained behavior.
Typical φ′ for low plasticity silts is 35–40° with little to no cohesion intercept.
CU triaxial tests on reconstituted specimens are often appropriate; failure criterion at Āf = 0 (zero excess pore pressure) is recommended for undrained tests.
UU triaxial tests on intact specimens are not advised due to scatter from disturbance.
Field tests are rarely appropriate due to uncertain drainage condition during testing.
USR formulas (ICU, ACU, DSS modes) allow estimation of su when φ′ is known and zero excess pore pressure at failure is assumed.
sections.applicability: Applies when characterizing shear strength of in situ nonplastic or low plasticity silt deposits (PI < 10, LL < 50) where conventional clay or sand methods are unreliable.

sections.title: Engineered Deposit of Fine-Grained Soil
sections.summary: Summarizes shear strength selection for compacted fine-grained fills used in embankments, dams, levees, and seepage barriers. Undrained strengths (from lab tests on compacted specimens) govern EOC, RDD, and seismic conditions. Drained strengths use peak parameters for PI < 20, LL < 40; fully softened strengths for higher plasticity soils.
sections.body:
Fine-grained soils are used as engineered fill in many different scenarios, including embankments, dams and levees, and seepage barriers. In many ways, the considerations for shear strength are similar to those for in situ deposits of fine-grained soil. The primary cases where undrained shear strength is required for fine-grained engineered fill are end-of-construction (EOC), rapid drawdown (RDD), and seismic analysis. Drained shear strengths are used for long-term conditions with peak strengths being appropriate for compacted fine-grained soils with PI < 20 and LL < 40. For soils with higher LL or PI, fully softened shear strengths should be considered for compacted slopes (Kayyal and Wright 1991) and retaining walls (Wright 2005). Methods for determining both undrained and drained shear strength of fine-grained engineered deposits are summarized in Table P-7 and Table P-8.

Undrained Shear Strength (Table P-7):
Laboratory tests on disturbed/compacted specimens – Very Appropriate. Specimens compacted to match field conditions. EOC: at least three UU triaxial tests per compaction combination; results interpreted as c–φ envelopes. RDD and Seismic: CU triaxial compression tests after saturation and consolidation to long-term condition; amount of swelling during saturation has substantial impact.

Laboratory tests on intact specimens – Often Appropriate. Intact specimens from existing fill can be tested using UU triaxial and other methods from Table P-4 for EOC parameters.

In situ or field tests – Rarely Appropriate. Not applicable except possibly for QA/QC during construction.

Correlations – Marginally Appropriate. Published correlations not useful for compacted fine-grained fill. Regional or soil-specific correlations (e.g., 15-point method) may be possible. Some correlations may apply to non-engineered fills in normally consolidated state (dredge spoils, mine tailings).

Drained Shear Strength (Table P-8):
Laboratory tests on disturbed/compacted specimens – Very Appropriate. Direct shear and CU triaxial tests on saturated specimens consolidated to a range of stresses. Drained strength parameters tend to be relatively insensitive to compaction state.

Laboratory tests on intact specimens – Often Appropriate. Direct shear or CU triaxial tests on intact specimens from existing fill.

In situ or field tests – Rarely Appropriate. Not applicable for compacted fine-grained soils.

Correlations – Sometimes Appropriate. Not useful for peak drained strength. Correlations from Table P-5 can estimate fully softened and residual strength parameters in some situations.
key_points: Undrained strength governs EOC, RDD, and seismic design cases for fine-grained engineered fills.
EOC undrained strength: at least 3 UU triaxial tests per compaction state; interpreted as c–φ envelopes.
RDD and seismic undrained strengths require CU triaxial tests after saturation and consolidation; swelling during saturation significantly affects results.
Peak drained strength is appropriate for long-term conditions when PI < 20 and LL < 40; fully softened strength should be used for higher plasticity soils.
Lab tests on compacted specimens are the primary method; in situ tests are only applicable for construction QA/QC.
Drained strength parameters for compacted fine-grained soils are relatively insensitive to compaction state.
Published correlations are generally not useful for compacted fine-grained fill, except for non-engineered fills in normally consolidated states.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining undrained or drained shear strength parameters for compacted fine-grained engineered fill in embankments, dams, levees, retaining walls, and seepage barriers.

Power function strength parameters (a, A, au, b, B, bu) define the shape and curvature of nonlinear failure envelopes.
Skempton's pore pressure parameter at failure (Āf) is explicitly listed, linking shear strength to consolidation behavior.
Undrained strength ratio (USR) and undrained shear strength (su) are separately defined, reflecting distinct strength characterization approaches.
Multiple friction angle variants are defined: peak (φʹp), residual (φʹR), fully softened (φʹFS), overconsolidated (φʹOC), and equivalent (φʹEQ).
Bearing capacity factors Nc, Nk, Nkt are defined specifically in the context of cone penetration interpretation of undrained strength.
Consolidation-related terms include coefficient of consolidation (cv), vertical consolidation stress (σʹ0), and major effective consolidation stress (σʹ1,con).
